title: Why You're Failing Assessment Centres (And How To Fix It)
description:
You're Solving The Wrong Test | How To Pass An Assessment Centre


Most people fail an assessment centre for one reason: they treat it as a test to solve, when it is a full day of your behaviour being observed and scored. If you keep reaching the assessment centre or the final-stage day and getting rejected, this video breaks down what assessors are actually marking and exactly how to pass an assessment centre.

You'll get the assessment centre group exercise strategy that gets you noticed for the right reasons, how to handle the case study and presentation so they score your thinking, and the prep that kills the nerves before you walk in.


What you'll learn in this video:
- Why competence is already screened before the assessment centre, and what assessors actually score on the day
- The exact assessment centre group exercise strategy: how to lead without dominating or disappearing
- The 5 behaviours on the assessor's scorecard, and how to hit each one
- How to handle the case study and presentation so they mark your thinking, not just your answer
- The prep that removes the unknowns, straight from the recruiter and Glassdoor, before you walk in


VIDEO CHAPTERS:
0:00 The real reason smart candidates fail
0:54 What an assessment centre actually scores
1:53 Shift 1: kill the unknowns before you walk in
2:26 Prep the format from the recruiter and Glassdoor
3:13 Shift 2: the group exercise most people lose
4:00 The dominate or disappear trap
4:25 How to lead the group without dominating
5:09 Shift 3: the case study and presentation
5:24 Why they score your thinking, not your answer
6:27 Cut your slides to one point
6:54 The whole day is the assessment
7:35 What to fix first


You don't pass an assessment centre by being the smartest person in the room. You pass it by fixing what is actually costing you points. Here's where to start:

FREE DIAGNOSIS:
Take the free 2-minute diagnosis. Get your personalised employability score plus a roadmap of exactly what to fix first in your job search.
https://the.offeraccelerator.uk/new-candidate-diagnosis?source=youtube&utm_source=youtube&utm_medium=description&utm_campaign=assessment-centre-wrong-test


CONNECT WITH ME
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/olivercordingley
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/olivercordingley


WATCH NEXT:
The Online Tests Rejecting You (Before Any Interview)


ABOUT ME:
I dropped out of university to build recruitment software and ATS systems used by hiring teams. For years I spoke to hundreds of hiring managers and recruiters every day, learning exactly how candidates get filtered, shortlisted, and hired from the inside. I started coaching friends through their job search using what I'd seen, then raised investment, built a software company, and hired my own team. I've seen hiring from every angle.

Today I help job seekers land offers faster using a proven 3-step system. I've coached hundreds of candidates into roles at firms like JP Morgan, Goldman Sachs, Deloitte, EY, and PwC and many more.

transcript: Every year, I watch people walk out of a PwC or a JP Morgan assessment center and they're certain that they smashed it because they got one or two right answers on the case. And then a week later, the rejection email lands and they've got no idea what went wrong. So, here is what went wrong. They spent the whole day trying to solve a test when the assessment center is really just a set up to watch how you behave. Now, the people scoring you aren't sitting there marking you whether, you know, you've cracked the case. They're sitting there with a sheet marking how you operate. Did you bring quieter people in? Did you handle disagreement well? Did you drive the group to a decision? That is the real reason smart candidates keep failing. And then once you get that, the whole day changes. You're not walking into a pass quiz. You're walking in to show them what you'd actually be like to work with. So, let me show you what they're actually really scoring and the three shifts that get you through the entire process. So, here's what an assessment center actually is. It's not one test. It's a full day where they stack a group exercise, a one-to-one interview, and usually a case study or a presentation, and sometimes a written task. And you'll probably have lunch or with the current team or something. And every single part of that is being watched and scored. Now, the mistake that almost everybody makes is is thinking that the scoring is about the competence. You know, things like whether you're clever enough, whether you got the numbers right. But by the time that you're actually at the assessment center, they've basically already screened for all of that. Your CV, your application, the online test, that was there to filter for whether you can actually do the job. So, the assessment center isn't asking if you can do it. It's asking what are you like to work with and have you got the room to grow? And that is what really matters because a hiring manager will almost always take a slightly less polished candidate who fits the team over just a more polished one who really doesn't. So, when you spend the day trying to look like the smartest person in the room, you're actually competing on the one thing that they've already kind of stopped looking at. So, the first shift is to kill the unknowns before you even walk in. And this is the one that nobody does. So, most of the fear that you feel at an assessment center isn't actually about ability. It's about really knowing what's actually coming up. And a candidate I was working with recently kept telling me that she just wasn't confident in interviews. And when we actually dug into it, the confidence wasn't the problem. She just didn't know the format, and she didn't know what they would actually ask. And she didn't really know what good look like. So, it's almost always the unknowns, and you can get rid of them quite easily. So, about 2 weeks before the day, email the recruiter and just ask them straight. Something like, "Could you walk me through the format of the day? Who I'll be meeting? And is there anything you'd recommend I prepare?" They'll almost always tell you before you ask that question because a candidate who performs well makes them look good. Then go ahead and read two or three interview reviews for that specific company on my website algen.uk, which is a free website where people write up the exact exercises that they got, the case, the group task, the presentation topic, you name it. So, by the time that you walk in, you already know the shape of the day whilst everyone else is trying to figure it out live. And that on its own is a massive edge. And look, like I'm not guessing any of this. Like, I've built the recruitment software that hiring teams have used to filter and score candidates. So, so I've seen the assessor side of this from the inside. And that's exactly why the next shift matters so much. So, that second shift is a big one, and it's the group exercise because that's where most people quietly lose. Now, the group exercise usually runs like this. They give your group a business problem, and then you've got about, you know, 10 to 20 minutes to roughly go through it, and then another 20 30 minutes to actually discuss it together, and then probably a 5 to 10-minute presentation at the end. And here's what everyone gets wrong. They treat it as competition. They think that the winner is whoever solves it or whoever just talks the most or whoever takes over. But the assessors aren't making the answer. They're literally sitting there with a sheet marking behaviors. You know, did you contribute something useful? Did you actually listen and build on other people? Did you bring the quiet ones in? Did you handle disagreement well? Did you keep an eye on the time? That is what they're scoring. So, what happens is is that people fall into one of two traps. The first is just being too dominating. You talk constantly, you interrupt, you try and solve the whole thing by yourself. And on that sheet, that reads as like doesn't really collaborate. Now, the second trap is the opposite. So, you're scared of coming across as domineering and that you'll go quiet and you'll only speak when someone asks you. Now, that reads as passive, no initiative. And most people sit at one of those two poles and both of them fail. So, the shift is to be the person who makes the group work better. So, right at the start before everyone dives in, you say something like this. Why don't we spend the first 5 minutes just understanding the problem and then, you know, 15-20 minutes generating options and then 5 deciding. Does that work with everyone else? And that one move makes you the leader without you ever having to assert dominance. Then, across the discussion, you deliberately do two or three things. So, you build on other people. So, to add to your point, then you bring the quiet ones in. So, we haven't heard from you yet. Like, what do you think? And then near the end, you drive it to a close. Ah, so we've got 5 minutes left. We need to land on the recommendation. Now, you don't need to be the loudest person in that room. You need to be the one that the assessors write down as the reason the group actually got somewhere. So, the third shift is for the case or the presentation. The bit where you have to work a problem or present something in front of them. And this is where the smartest candidates often trip up because they think it's all about the content. It's actually most entirely about how you communicated it. So, here's the thing that they don't tell you. In a case, the interviewer isn't expecting you to get the right answer. What they care about is your thinking. So, the worst thing that you can do is just go quiet, work it all out in your head and then present the final answer. Because if it's wrong, they've got nothing to score you on. And if you get stuck, you just look stuck. So, instead, you narrate. You literally talk them through it. You say, "Okay, here's how I'm thinking about this. First, I'd look at this and then this and that's what tells me this. And a candidate I worked with kept getting stuck in his own head and going silent. And then the feedback was basically, "The problem is that you're talking to yourself, not to me. So, you make sure you talk to the assessor." So, even when you're not certain, say your next step out loud and keep moving. And there's a mindset underneath this entire thing, and it takes the pressure off. But most of these cases, they're not expecting you to be an expert in the industry. They just want to see how you break down a problem, you know, how you interpret information, and whether you actually a bit of initiative. So, you don't need the perfect answer. You just need to think out loud like someone that they would trust to figure it out on your own when you get the job. Then when you present, cut it down hard. And most people cram five points onto every slide and then try and say everything. But when you strip it back to one clear point, it does two things at once. One, you're going to feel more confident because you're not drowning in your own notes. And what happens is they actually listen instead of getting distracted by reading a wall of text. So, give them one thing to remember, not five. And it protects you as well because the more you say, the more open you are to actually being asked a question that you can't answer. And then one last thing that catches loads of people out, the whole day is the assessment. The coffee at the start, the lunch with the team, how you treat the person at the reception. Assessors talk to each other, and those relaxed moments are where people actually switch off and are often exactly where it's actually decided. So, treat every single interaction as part of it because it is. So, that's it. Like, you don't pass the assessment center by being the smartest person in the room. You pass it by knowing exactly what is being scored and then showing them what you'd actually be like to work with. Kill the unknowns before you go in, make the group work better instead of trying to win it, and then talk them through your thinking instead of just chasing the right answer. Now, if you want to see exactly where you're losing points in your own job search right now, whether that's your CV, your applications, or how you're coming across at this stage, I built a free 2-minute diagnosis that it gives you a personalized breakdown of what to do first and what to fix. And the link is in the description, so go ahead and do that and make sure you get that offer.
